title: You Co-Signed to Be Nice. Now the Whole Loan Is Yours
alts: Your Friend's Car Loan Can Wreck YOUR Credit (Co-Signing)
Why Co-Signing for a Friend Makes YOU the Borrower
line1: What happens when you co-sign a loan and they stop paying? Dave co-signed his buddy's car loan. Then a debt collector called him.
summary: Dave co-signs his buddy Bob's $18,000 car loan as a favor. Six months later a debt collector calls Dave about a car he has never driven. We follow the whole story: why a co-signer is a second borrower, not a reference; how the co-signed loan lands on Dave's own credit report and even counts against his mortgage application; how Bob's late payments hit Dave's record; why the lender can come straight to Dave without chasing Bob first (FTC); what a CreditCards.com survey found about how often co-signers end up paying (38%); why lenders rarely let a co-signer go (CFPB: 90% of release requests rejected); and the repossession math that could have left Dave owing $7,000 for a car that's gone. Then how Dave fought back, and the one sentence printed on the paper he signed.
